fieldFixes.description: Principles-based and voluntary between states: the APEC Privacy Framework (2004) asks each economy to implement nine principles as it sees fit, with a strong emphasis on not obstructing information flows. issues: Overgeneralised: 'personal data is treated as a national resource that must be stored at home or exported only after state security review'. PIPL Art. 40 applies the store-at-home and security-assessment rule only to critical information infrastructure operators and processors above CAC volume thresholds. Other processors may export under Art. 38 by standard contract or certification. Russia's 242-FZ requires citizens' data to be recorded and stored in databases in Russia, but it does not impose a state security review on export.
The PIPL quote was cut off before the sentence that actually carries the 'security review' claim. It is extended with '确需向境外提供的，应当通过国家网信部门组织的安全评估' (--check FOUND).
'The state keeps broad access for security purposes' had no support. A Bradford excerpt quote from the same ProMarket page is added.

Verified: 242-FZ is dated 21.07.2014 and came into force 1 September 2015 (kremlin.ru). It amends 152-FZ of 27 July 2006, which confirms the '152-FZ 2006' exemplar. PIPL was adopted 20 Aug 2021 and in force 1 Nov 2021 (Art. 74). ProMarket excerpt date 2024-04-11 (article:published_time).

fieldFixes.description: Strong rules bind companies, often with GDPR-like individual rights, but the state keeps broad access for security purposes, and personal data is treated as a national resource: Russia requires its citizens' data to be recorded and stored in databases inside the country, and China requires critical operators and large-volume processors to store data at home and pass a state security assessment before exporting it. Russia's 2014 localisation law and China's Cybersecurity Law (2016) and PIPL (2021) are the defining cases; Bradford calls China's version 'state-driven'. Several other countries have since copied localisation or security-assessment rules.

fieldFixes.description: The individual gets a constitutional writ, modelled on habeas corpus, to go to court, see what a databank holds about them, and demand correction or deletion. It is a remedy the person sets in motion rather than a regulator's licensing system. Brazil created it in 1988; Paraguay (1992), Peru (1993) and Argentina (1994) followed, then Ecuador and Colombia. General data-protection statutes and regulators came later: Argentina's law in 2000 (its regulator set up under a 2001 decree) and Brazil's LGPD in 2018.

issues: Misattribution. The correction says 'India's Supreme Court, rejecting the argument that privacy is an elitist construct, traced a well-developed sense of privacy in ancient Indian and Islamic sources'. The 'elitist construct' rejection is in Chandrachud J's plurality (Part O, 'Not an elitist construct'). The ancient-texts and Islam passages (para 23) are in S.A. Bobde J's separate concurring judgment, not the Court's opinion.

The Tokyo 1964 example cuts against the correction as written. The record's own JILPT source says Japan adopted the American 'right to be let alone' concept 'after the introduction of this theory by academics in the 1960s'. So the ruling shows an imported (American) idea, not an indigenous one. It still rebuts 'exported with European law', so it is kept and reworded to say so.

'172 countries ... most of them outside Europe' and 'habeas data from 1988' had no source on this record. Sources are added: Greenleaf/PL&B 2025 (172 by March 2025), Greenleaf/PL&B 2017 ('European laws (54/120) are a decreasing minority') and Guadamuz (Brazil 1988).
Verdict MISLEADING stands.

fieldFixes.correction: The first data-protection statutes were European, but concern for privacy is much older and wider. In the 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, India's Supreme Court rejected the argument that privacy is an 'elitist construct', and Justice Bobde's concurring opinion traced a well-developed sense of privacy in ancient Indian texts and in Islam. A Tokyo court recognised a right to privacy in 1964, drawing on American theory rather than European law, and Latin America built its own constitutional remedy, habeas data, from 1988. European laws were already a minority of the world's data-privacy laws by 2017, and by March 2025 Greenleaf counted 172 countries with such laws.

fieldFixes.correction: Greenleaf's census counted 172 countries with national data-privacy laws by March 2025, and new laws have been added at 5.4 a year since 2020. His count includes some jurisdictions that are not UN members (in 2018, 112 of his 124 were UN member states), so it is not a straight comparison with the 193 UN member states, but a majority of UN members already had such laws by 2018 (112 of 193) and the share has grown since. Coverage and enforcement vary widely, and some large states (for example Pakistan) still have only a bill, but having no law at all is now the exception.
